transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

My thoughts won’t slow down—they’re racing all the time and I can’t turn them off long enough to focus or rest. It feels like my mind is running too fast to keep up with, and I just can't find a way to quiet it down.
Are these racing thoughts mostly uncontrollable worries about everyday life, or do they feel more like a rapid flow of different ideas, perhaps accompanied by high energy?

It’s definitely more of a rapid flow of creative ideas and plans, like my brain is a pinball machine jumping from one thought to another. I get this buzzing, amped-up energy where I'm constantly starting new projects and feel like I can't sit still. It's not really about everyday worries, just this overwhelming rush of thoughts.
Have you struggled with this high energy and racing thoughts since childhood, or does this happen in distinct periods that last for a few days or weeks at a time?

No, this isn't something I've struggled with since childhood—it actually started about a year ago after I transitioned to full-time freelance work. It comes in these intense, distinct stretches of a few days or weeks where I feel completely amped up and barely sleep, rather than being a constant thing.
Have you ever experienced periods in your life where you felt the opposite—very down, empty, or completely lost interest in things for weeks at a time?

No, I haven't really experienced prolonged periods of feeling deeply down, empty, or losing interest in things. Sometimes I'll feel really flat or physically exhausted and crashed after one of my high-energy stretches, but it doesn't feel like a deep, lasting depression.
Have you experienced multiple separate periods of this high energy with times of feeling back to your normal self in between, or is this current stretch the very first time it has happened?

No, this isn't the first time at all. I've had these intense, high-energy periods on and off for about a year now, ever since I transitioned to full-time freelance work. I only get short, temporary stretches in between where I feel closer to my normal baseline before the buzzing energy starts right back up again.
During these high-energy phases, have you ever made impulsive decisions, spent excessive money, or taken risks that caused problems in your work or relationships?

I haven't really spent excessive money or taken major physical risks, though I have impulsively taken on too many projects at once and emailed venues at 3 a.m. without thinking it through. That impulsiveness has definitely strained some of my professional relationships and caused me to miss important deadlines.
During these high-energy phases, have they ever been so intense that you needed hospital care, or did family and friends become extremely concerned for your safety?

No, I’ve never been hospitalized or needed hospital care. But my roommate and friends got really concerned because I've been pulling away and letting basic things like chores and eating slide, to the point where my roommate had to step in and help. It was actually a close friend who noticed how intense my behavior was getting and helped me set up this appointment.
During these high-energy phases, are you using any recreational drugs, stimulants, or high amounts of caffeine, or do you have any medical conditions like thyroid issues?
No, I don't use any recreational drugs, stimulants, or even much caffeine, and I don't have any medical conditions like thyroid issues. All of this is just happening on its own.
When you have these high-energy periods, how long do they typically last—do they usually last for just a few days, or do they consistently go on for a full week or longer?

They consistently last for a week or longer, often stretching into several weeks at a time. During these periods, I can go for weeks sleeping only about three hours a night and feeling completely wired, with only short breaks before I crash or temporarily return to my normal baseline.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent episodes of elevated energy, racing thoughts, decreased need for sleep, and increased goal-directed activity/impulsivity lasting a week or longer. These episodes cause significant functional impairment, including neglecting basic self-care (eating and chores) to the point of requiring roommate intervention, as well as occupational impairment (strained professional relationships and missed deadlines). There is no history of major depressive episodes or substance/medical etiology. The severity of impairment and duration of episodes support a manic episode rather than a hypomanic episode, leading to a diagnosis of Bipolar affective disorder, current episode manic without psychotic symptoms (F31.1).
